title: Microbiology: Bacteria, Viruses, Fungi
description: For biology and health-science learners studying microbial structures, growth, genetics, viruses, fungi, and laboratory concepts. Educational consensus only; verify with current guidelines for clinical applications.

sources.name: Original educational wording from general knowledge

cards.back: An organism whose cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes.
cards.example: Where is most bacterial chromosomal DNA located? In the nucleoid, a region not enclosed by a nuclear membrane.

cards.front: Where is most bacterial chromosomal DNA located?
cards.back: In the nucleoid, a region not enclosed by a nuclear membrane.
cards.example: Define: Prokaryote An organism whose cells lack a membrane-bound nucleus; bacteria and archaea are prokaryotes.

cards.back: An organism with cells containing a membrane-bound nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.
cards.example: Are fungi prokaryotic or eukaryotic? Eukaryotic; their cells contain nuclei and organelles.

cards.back: Eukaryotic; their cells contain nuclei and organelles.
cards.example: Define: Eukaryote An organism with cells containing a membrane-bound nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.

cards.back: A cellular prokaryotic organism; bacteria have diverse metabolisms and many have peptidoglycan cell walls.
cards.example: Are all bacteria pathogenic? No. Many are harmless, beneficial, or essential to ecosystems.

cards.back: No. Many are harmless, beneficial, or essential to ecosystems.
cards.example: Define: Bacterium A cellular prokaryotic organism; bacteria have diverse metabolisms and many have peptidoglycan cell walls.

cards.back: A prokaryote in a domain distinct from Bacteria, with characteristic membrane chemistry and no true peptidoglycan.
cards.example: Does absence of a nucleus distinguish bacteria from archaea? No. Both lack a membrane-bound nucleus; other molecular features distinguish them.

cards.front: Does absence of a nucleus distinguish bacteria from archaea?
cards.back: No. Both lack a membrane-bound nucleus; other molecular features distinguish them.
cards.example: Define: Archaeon A prokaryote in a domain distinct from Bacteria, with characteristic membrane chemistry and no true peptidoglycan.

cards.back: An acellular infectious agent with a nucleic acid genome that requires host cells to produce new virions.
cards.example: Why can viruses not replicate on ordinary cell-free nutrient agar? They depend on living host-cell machinery rather than carrying out independent cellular reproduction.

cards.front: Why can viruses not replicate on ordinary cell-free nutrient agar?
cards.back: They depend on living host-cell machinery rather than carrying out independent cellular reproduction.
cards.example: Define: Virus An acellular infectious agent with a nucleic acid genome that requires host cells to produce new virions.

cards.back: A complete virus particle outside a host cell, consisting of a genome and capsid, sometimes with an envelope.
cards.example: How does a virion differ from an infected cell? A virion is a particle carrying the viral genome; an infected cell is the living cellular environment used for replication.

cards.front: How does a virion differ from an infected cell?
cards.back: A virion is a particle carrying the viral genome; an infected cell is the living cellular environment used for replication.
cards.example: Define: Virion A complete virus particle outside a host cell, consisting of a genome and capsid, sometimes with an envelope.

cards.back: A protein shell that encloses a viral genome.
cards.example: What are capsomeres? Morphological protein subunits of a viral capsid.

cards.back: Morphological protein subunits of a viral capsid.
cards.example: Define: Capsid A protein shell that encloses a viral genome.

cards.back: A lipid-containing outer layer acquired from host membranes and containing viral proteins.
cards.example: Why are many enveloped viruses vulnerable to soaps and detergents? Disruption of their lipid envelope can prevent them from entering cells effectively.

cards.front: Why are many enveloped viruses vulnerable to soaps and detergents?
cards.back: Disruption of their lipid envelope can prevent them from entering cells effectively.
cards.example: Define: Viral envelope A lipid-containing outer layer acquired from host membranes and containing viral proteins.

cards.back: A virus that infects bacteria.
cards.example: What type of host does a phage infect? A bacterial cell, usually within a specific host range.

cards.front: What type of host does a phage infect?
cards.back: A bacterial cell, usually within a specific host range.
cards.example: Define: Bacteriophage A virus that infects bacteria.

cards.back: The set of host species or cell types a microbe or virus can infect.
cards.example: How can receptor compatibility affect viral host range? A virus often requires compatible surface receptors to attach and enter a cell.

cards.front: How can receptor compatibility affect viral host range?
cards.back: A virus often requires compatible surface receptors to attach and enter a cell.
cards.example: Define: Host range The set of host species or cell types a microbe or virus can infect.

cards.back: Preference of a pathogen for particular cells or tissues.
cards.example: Why can two viruses infect different tissues in the same person? Receptor availability, intracellular compatibility, and local defenses can differ among tissues.

cards.front: Why can two viruses infect different tissues in the same person?
cards.back: Receptor availability, intracellular compatibility, and local defenses can differ among tissues.
cards.example: Define: Tropism Preference of a pathogen for particular cells or tissues.

cards.back: A phage replication cycle that produces new particles and typically lyses the host cell.
cards.example: What happens to a bacterium at the end of a typical lytic phage cycle? The cell ruptures and releases progeny phages.

cards.front: What happens to a bacterium at the end of a typical lytic phage cycle?
cards.back: The cell ruptures and releases progeny phages.
cards.example: Define: Lytic cycle A phage replication cycle that produces new particles and typically lyses the host cell.

cards.back: A state in which a temperate phage genome persists in a host without immediately producing lysis.
cards.example: What is a prophage? A phage genome maintained in a bacterium, often integrated into its chromosome.

cards.back: A phage genome maintained in a bacterium, often integrated into its chromosome.
cards.example: Define: Lysogeny A state in which a temperate phage genome persists in a host without immediately producing lysis.

cards.back: An RNA virus that uses reverse transcriptase to produce a DNA intermediate.
cards.example: What reaction does reverse transcriptase perform? It synthesizes DNA using RNA as a template.

cards.front: What reaction does reverse transcriptase perform?
cards.back: It synthesizes DNA using RNA as a template.
cards.example: Define: Retrovirus An RNA virus that uses reverse transcriptase to produce a DNA intermediate.

cards.back: A viral RNA genome that can function as messenger RNA after entering a suitable host cell.
cards.example: Can positive-sense viral RNA generally be translated directly by host ribosomes? Yes, once accessible in a compatible host cell; replication still requires additional viral processes.

cards.front: Can positive-sense viral RNA generally be translated directly by host ribosomes?
cards.back: Yes, once accessible in a compatible host cell; replication still requires additional viral processes.
cards.example: Define: Positive-sense RNA genome A viral RNA genome that can function as messenger RNA after entering a suitable host cell.

cards.back: A viral RNA genome complementary to the messenger RNA needed for translation.
cards.example: Why must negative-sense RNA viruses supply an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion? The host cannot directly translate the negative-sense genome or make the required complementary viral mRNA on its own.

cards.front: Why must negative-sense RNA viruses supply an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in the virion?
cards.back: The host cannot directly translate the negative-sense genome or make the required complementary viral mRNA on its own.
cards.example: Define: Negative-sense RNA genome A viral RNA genome complementary to the messenger RNA needed for translation.

cards.back: A genome divided among separate nucleic acid molecules.
cards.example: What process can exchange whole genome segments between related viruses in a coinfected cell? Reassortment.

cards.front: What process can exchange whole genome segments between related viruses in a coinfected cell?
cards.back: Reassortment.
cards.example: Define: Segmented viral genome A genome divided among separate nucleic acid molecules.

cards.back: Gradual antigenic change resulting from accumulated mutations.
cards.example: Why can influenza immunity become less effective over time? Mutations can change viral antigens, reducing recognition by existing immune responses.

cards.front: Why can influenza immunity become less effective over time?
cards.back: Mutations can change viral antigens, reducing recognition by existing immune responses.
cards.example: Define: Antigenic drift Gradual antigenic change resulting from accumulated mutations.

cards.front: Define: Antigenic shift in influenza A
cards.back: A major antigenic change, often involving reassortment of genome segments.
cards.example: Which influenza type is classically associated with antigenic shift and pandemic emergence? Influenza A; reassortment can create substantially different surface antigen combinations.

cards.front: Which influenza type is classically associated with antigenic shift and pandemic emergence?
cards.back: Influenza A; reassortment can create substantially different surface antigen combinations.
cards.example: Define: Antigenic shift in influenza A A major antigenic change, often involving reassortment of genome segments.

cards.back: Persistence of an infection with limited productive replication and the possibility of later reactivation.
cards.example: How is latent infection different from pathogen elimination? The pathogen or its genome remains and can potentially reactivate.

cards.front: How is latent infection different from pathogen elimination?
cards.back: The pathogen or its genome remains and can potentially reactivate.
cards.example: Define: Latency Persistence of an infection with limited productive replication and the possibility of later reactivation.

cards.back: An infectious misfolded protein that promotes misfolding of normal versions of the protein.
cards.example: What usual infectious-agent component do prions lack? A nucleic acid genome.

cards.front: What usual infectious-agent component do prions lack?
cards.back: A nucleic acid genome.
cards.example: Define: Prion An infectious misfolded protein that promotes misfolding of normal versions of the protein.

cards.back: A roughly spherical bacterial cell shape.
cards.example: What does the prefix strepto- suggest in a bacterial arrangement? Cells arranged in chains.

cards.front: What does the prefix strepto- suggest in a bacterial arrangement?
cards.back: Cells arranged in chains.
cards.example: Define: Coccus A roughly spherical bacterial cell shape.

cards.back: A rod-shaped bacterial cell, distinct from the capitalized genus name Bacillus.
cards.example: What does the prefix staphylo- suggest in a bacterial arrangement? Irregular clusters of cells, often compared with grapes.

cards.front: What does the prefix staphylo- suggest in a bacterial arrangement?
cards.back: Irregular clusters of cells, often compared with grapes.
cards.example: Define: Bacillus, as a shape A rod-shaped bacterial cell, distinct from the capitalized genus name Bacillus.

cards.back: A flexible, helically shaped bacterium with internal axial filaments used for motility.
cards.example: How do spirochetes move through viscous environments? Their endoflagella generate twisting or corkscrew-like movement.

cards.front: How do spirochetes move through viscous environments?
cards.back: Their endoflagella generate twisting or corkscrew-like movement.
cards.example: Define: Spirochete A flexible, helically shaped bacterium with internal axial filaments used for motility.

cards.back: A bacterial wall polymer of sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides.
cards.example: Is peptidoglycan a normal component of human cell membranes? No. It is a bacterial cell-wall component, making its synthesis a selective antimicrobial target.

cards.front: Is peptidoglycan a normal component of human cell membranes?
cards.back: No. It is a bacterial cell-wall component, making its synthesis a selective antimicrobial target.
cards.example: Define: Peptidoglycan A bacterial wall polymer of sugar chains cross-linked by short peptides.

cards.back: An envelope typically containing a thick peptidoglycan layer without a Gram-negative-type outer membrane.
cards.example: What color do typical Gram-positive cells retain after a correct Gram stain? Purple, because they retain the crystal violet-iodine complex during decolorization.

cards.front: What color do typical Gram-positive cells retain after a correct Gram stain?
cards.back: Purple, because they retain the crystal violet-iodine complex during decolorization.
cards.example: Define: Gram-positive cell envelope An envelope typically containing a thick peptidoglycan layer without a Gram-negative-type outer membrane.

cards.back: An envelope with thin peptidoglycan and an outer membrane that usually contains lipopolysaccharide.
cards.example: What color do typical Gram-negative cells appear after counterstaining? Pink or red, commonly from safranin after losing the primary stain during decolorization.

cards.front: What color do typical Gram-negative cells appear after counterstaining?
cards.back: Pink or red, commonly from safranin after losing the primary stain during decolorization.
cards.example: Define: Gram-negative cell envelope An envelope with thin peptidoglycan and an outer membrane that usually contains lipopolysaccharide.

cards.back: A major outer-membrane component of many Gram-negative bacteria, composed of lipid A and sugar regions.
cards.example: Which part of lipopolysaccharide accounts for its endotoxin activity? Lipid A.

cards.front: Which part of lipopolysaccharide accounts for its endotoxin activity?
cards.back: Lipid A.
cards.example: Define: Lipopolysaccharide A major outer-membrane component of many Gram-negative bacteria, composed of lipid A and sugar regions.

cards.back: A staining approach that detects cells retaining dye after acid-alcohol treatment, classically mycobacteria.
cards.example: Which wall lipids contribute to mycobacterial acid-fastness? Mycolic acids.

cards.front: Which wall lipids contribute to mycobacterial acid-fastness?
cards.back: Mycolic acids.
cards.example: Define: Acid-fast staining A staining approach that detects cells retaining dye after acid-alcohol treatment, classically mycobacteria.

cards.back: An organized external layer, often polysaccharide, surrounding some microbial cells.
cards.example: How can a bacterial capsule contribute to virulence? It may inhibit phagocytosis and promote attachment or persistence.

cards.front: How can a bacterial capsule contribute to virulence?
cards.back: It may inhibit phagocytosis and promote attachment or persistence.
cards.example: Define: Capsule An organized external layer, often polysaccharide, surrounding some microbial cells.

cards.back: A motility appendage; bacterial flagella usually rotate.
cards.example: What is chemotaxis? Directed movement in response to chemical gradients, such as movement toward a nutrient.

cards.back: Directed movement in response to chemical gradients, such as movement toward a nutrient.
cards.example: Define: Flagellum A motility appendage; bacterial flagella usually rotate.

cards.back: A short bacterial surface appendage commonly involved in attachment.
cards.example: How can attachment structures help a bacterium establish colonization? They allow cells to adhere to surfaces instead of being washed away.

cards.front: How can attachment structures help a bacterium establish colonization?
cards.back: They allow cells to adhere to surfaces instead of being washed away.
cards.example: Define: Fimbria A short bacterial surface appendage commonly involved in attachment.

cards.back: A bacterial appendage involved in cell contact during certain forms of DNA transfer.
cards.example: Does all bacterial DNA transfer require a pilus? No. Transformation and transduction use different mechanisms.

cards.front: Does all bacterial DNA transfer require a pilus?
cards.back: No. Transformation and transduction use different mechanisms.
cards.example: Define: Conjugative pilus A bacterial appendage involved in cell contact during certain forms of DNA transfer.

cards.back: A dormant, highly resistant structure formed by some bacteria for survival.
cards.example: Is bacterial endospore formation a reproductive process that increases cell number? No. One cell forms one endospore, which can later germinate into one vegetative cell.

cards.front: Is bacterial endospore formation a reproductive process that increases cell number?
cards.back: No. One cell forms one endospore, which can later germinate into one vegetative cell.
cards.example: Define: Endospore A dormant, highly resistant structure formed by some bacteria for survival.

cards.back: Cell division in which one bacterial cell produces two daughter cells after genome replication.
cards.example: In ideal binary fission, how many descendants arise after three divisions from one cell? Eight, assuming every descendant divides and none die.

cards.front: In ideal binary fission, how many descendants arise after three divisions from one cell?
cards.back: Eight, assuming every descendant divides and none die.
cards.example: Define: Binary fission Cell division in which one bacterial cell produces two daughter cells after genome replication.

cards.back: The time required for a population to double under specified conditions.
cards.example: Is generation time fixed for a bacterial species in all environments? No. Nutrients, temperature, and other conditions affect it.

cards.front: Is generation time fixed for a bacterial species in all environments?
cards.back: No. Nutrients, temperature, and other conditions affect it.
cards.example: Define: Generation time The time required for a population to double under specified conditions.

cards.back: An initial growth phase in which cells adapt to conditions with little net population increase.
cards.example: Can cells be metabolically active during lag phase? Yes. They may synthesize enzymes and cellular components before rapid division.

cards.front: Can cells be metabolically active during lag phase?
cards.back: Yes. They may synthesize enzymes and cellular components before rapid division.
cards.example: Define: Lag phase An initial growth phase in which cells adapt to conditions with little net population increase.

cards.back: A phase of exponential population growth under favorable conditions.
cards.example: On a graph of log cell number against time, how does ideal exponential growth appear? As an approximately straight rising line.

cards.front: On a graph of log cell number against time, how does ideal exponential growth appear?
cards.back: As an approximately straight rising line.
cards.example: Define: Log phase A phase of exponential population growth under favorable conditions.

cards.back: A phase in which net population size stabilizes as resource limits and waste affect growth.
cards.example: Does stationary phase mean every cell has stopped all metabolic activity? No. Cells may remain active, and growth and death can roughly balance.

cards.front: Does stationary phase mean every cell has stopped all metabolic activity?
cards.back: No. Cells may remain active, and growth and death can roughly balance.
cards.example: Define: Stationary phase A phase in which net population size stabilizes as resource limits and waste affect growth.

cards.back: A phase in which viable cell numbers decline.
cards.example: What is the difference between a total cell count and a viable count? A total count can include dead cells; a viable count estimates cells able to reproduce under the assay conditions.

cards.front: What is the difference between a total cell count and a viable count?
cards.back: A total count can include dead cells; a viable count estimates cells able to reproduce under the assay conditions.
cards.example: Define: Death phase A phase in which viable cell numbers decline.

cards.back: An organism that requires oxygen for growth.
cards.example: Where would an obligate aerobe tend to grow in an oxygen-gradient broth? Near the oxygen-rich surface.

cards.front: Where would an obligate aerobe tend to grow in an oxygen-gradient broth?
cards.back: Near the oxygen-rich surface.
cards.example: Define: Obligate aerobe An organism that requires oxygen for growth.

cards.back: An organism that cannot grow in oxygen under its usual conditions and may be harmed by it.
cards.example: Why is oxygen exposure a concern when culturing strict anaerobes? It can inhibit or kill them, making recovery unreliable.

cards.front: Why is oxygen exposure a concern when culturing strict anaerobes?
cards.back: It can inhibit or kill them, making recovery unreliable.
cards.example: Define: Obligate anaerobe An organism that cannot grow in oxygen under its usual conditions and may be harmed by it.

cards.back: An organism that can grow with or without oxygen, often growing better with it.
cards.example: How does a facultative anaerobe differ from an obligate aerobe? It can grow without oxygen, whereas an obligate aerobe requires oxygen.

cards.front: How does a facultative anaerobe differ from an obligate aerobe?
cards.back: It can grow without oxygen, whereas an obligate aerobe requires oxygen.
cards.example: Define: Facultative anaerobe An organism that can grow with or without oxygen, often growing better with it.

cards.back: An organism requiring oxygen at levels below atmospheric concentration.
cards.example: Why is ordinary room air not always suitable for a microaerophile? Its oxygen concentration can be too high for optimal growth.

cards.front: Why is ordinary room air not always suitable for a microaerophile?
cards.back: Its oxygen concentration can be too high for optimal growth.
cards.example: Define: Microaerophile An organism requiring oxygen at levels below atmospheric concentration.

cards.back: An organism that does not use oxygen for energy metabolism but tolerates its presence.
cards.example: How does an aerotolerant anaerobe differ from a facultative anaerobe? It tolerates oxygen without using aerobic respiration for growth.

cards.front: How does an aerotolerant anaerobe differ from a facultative anaerobe?
cards.back: It tolerates oxygen without using aerobic respiration for growth.
cards.example: Define: Aerotolerant anaerobe An organism that does not use oxygen for energy metabolism but tolerates its presence.

cards.back: A community of microbes attached to a surface and embedded in a self-produced matrix.
cards.example: Why can a biofilm be harder to eradicate than free-living cells? The matrix, altered metabolism, and community structure can reduce antimicrobial susceptibility and immune clearance.

cards.front: Why can a biofilm be harder to eradicate than free-living cells?
cards.back: The matrix, altered metabolism, and community structure can reduce antimicrobial susceptibility and immune clearance.
cards.example: Define: Biofilm A community of microbes attached to a surface and embedded in a self-produced matrix.

cards.back: Regulation of microbial behavior through signaling molecules whose concentration reflects population conditions.
cards.example: What can quorum sensing help coordinate? Group behaviors such as biofilm formation or production of virulence factors.

cards.front: What can quorum sensing help coordinate?
cards.back: Group behaviors such as biofilm formation or production of virulence factors.
cards.example: Define: Quorum sensing Regulation of microbial behavior through signaling molecules whose concentration reflects population conditions.

cards.back: A replicating DNA molecule separate from the main chromosome, often circular in bacteria.
cards.example: Can plasmids carry antimicrobial resistance genes? Yes. Some also carry virulence or metabolic genes and can move between cells.

cards.front: Can plasmids carry antimicrobial resistance genes?
cards.back: Yes. Some also carry virulence or metabolic genes and can move between cells.
cards.example: Define: Plasmid A replicating DNA molecule separate from the main chromosome, often circular in bacteria.

cards.back: Uptake of free environmental DNA by a competent cell.
cards.example: What DNA source is used in bacterial transformation? Naked extracellular DNA rather than DNA delivered by a phage or direct donor-cell contact.

cards.front: What DNA source is used in bacterial transformation?
cards.back: Naked extracellular DNA rather than DNA delivered by a phage or direct donor-cell contact.
cards.example: Define: Transformation Uptake of free environmental DNA by a competent cell.

cards.back: Transfer of bacterial DNA mediated by a bacteriophage.
cards.example: What carries DNA from one bacterium to another in transduction? A phage particle.

cards.front: What carries DNA from one bacterium to another in transduction?
cards.back: A phage particle.
cards.example: Define: Transduction Transfer of bacterial DNA mediated by a bacteriophage.

cards.back: DNA transfer requiring direct contact between donor and recipient cells.
cards.example: How does conjugation differ from binary fission? Conjugation transfers genetic material; binary fission increases cell number.

cards.front: How does conjugation differ from binary fission?
cards.back: Conjugation transfers genetic material; binary fission increases cell number.
cards.example: Define: Conjugation DNA transfer requiring direct contact between donor and recipient cells.

cards.back: A change in a genetic sequence.
cards.example: Do bacteria intentionally mutate to acquire the specific resistance they need? No. Mutations arise without foresight; selection can enrich variants that survive exposure.

cards.front: Do bacteria intentionally mutate to acquire the specific resistance they need?
cards.back: No. Mutations arise without foresight; selection can enrich variants that survive exposure.
cards.example: Define: Mutation A change in a genetic sequence.

cards.back: Movement of genes between organisms outside parent-to-offspring inheritance.
cards.example: Name three common mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer in bacteria. Transformation, transduction, and conjugation.

cards.front: Name three common mechanisms of horizontal gene transfer in bacteria.
cards.back: Transformation, transduction, and conjugation.
cards.example: Define: Horizontal gene transfer Movement of genes between organisms outside parent-to-offspring inheritance.

cards.back: A culture medium that favors some organisms while inhibiting others.
cards.example: What distinguishes selective from differential media? Selective media restrict growth; differential media reveal biochemical differences. A medium can do both.

cards.front: What distinguishes selective from differential media?
cards.back: Selective media restrict growth; differential media reveal biochemical differences. A medium can do both.
cards.example: Define: Selective medium A culture medium that favors some organisms while inhibiting others.

cards.back: A medium that makes distinct microbial properties visible, often through color changes.
cards.example: Why are indicator dyes useful in differential media? They can reveal chemical changes, such as acid production from sugar fermentation.

cards.front: Why are indicator dyes useful in differential media?
cards.back: They can reveal chemical changes, such as acid production from sugar fermentation.
cards.example: Define: Differential medium A medium that makes distinct microbial properties visible, often through color changes.

cards.back: A unit estimated from growth of a colony, potentially arising from one viable cell or a cell cluster.
cards.example: Why is one colony not always equivalent to one original bacterial cell? A clump or chain of cells can produce a single colony.

cards.front: Why is one colony not always equivalent to one original bacterial cell?
cards.back: A clump or chain of cells can produce a single colony.
cards.example: Define: Colony-forming unit A unit estimated from growth of a colony, potentially arising from one viable cell or a cell cluster.

cards.back: A culture containing one microbial type, ideally derived from an isolated colony.
cards.example: Why is isolation important for identifying an organism's traits? Mixed organisms can produce combined results that are incorrectly attributed to one species.

cards.front: Why is isolation important for identifying an organism's traits?
cards.back: Mixed organisms can produce combined results that are incorrectly attributed to one species.
cards.example: Define: Pure culture A culture containing one microbial type, ideally derived from an isolated colony.

cards.back: Practices intended to minimize unwanted microbial contamination.
cards.example: Is aseptic technique the same as proof that everything is sterile? No. It reduces contamination risk but does not itself demonstrate sterility.

cards.front: Is aseptic technique the same as proof that everything is sterile?
cards.back: No. It reduces contamination risk but does not itself demonstrate sterility.
cards.example: Define: Aseptic technique Practices intended to minimize unwanted microbial contamination.

cards.back: A validated process that eliminates viable microorganisms, including bacterial endospores.
cards.example: How does sterilization differ from routine disinfection? Disinfection does not necessarily eliminate all microorganisms or bacterial endospores.

cards.front: How does sterilization differ from routine disinfection?
cards.back: Disinfection does not necessarily eliminate all microorganisms or bacterial endospores.
cards.example: Define: Sterilization A validated process that eliminates viable microorganisms, including bacterial endospores.

cards.back: Reduction or elimination of many pathogens on inanimate surfaces, with effectiveness depending on the method.
cards.example: Where are disinfectants generally used, as distinct from antiseptics? On nonliving surfaces; antiseptics are formulated for living tissue.

cards.front: Where are disinfectants generally used, as distinct from antiseptics?
cards.back: On nonliving surfaces; antiseptics are formulated for living tissue.
cards.example: Define: Disinfection Reduction or elimination of many pathogens on inanimate surfaces, with effectiveness depending on the method.

cards.back: A device using pressurized steam for a validated sterilization cycle.
cards.example: Why does pressure matter in steam sterilization? It allows saturated steam to reach temperatures above the normal boiling point; appropriate exposure conditions must be validated.

cards.front: Why does pressure matter in steam sterilization?
cards.back: It allows saturated steam to reach temperatures above the normal boiling point; appropriate exposure conditions must be validated.
cards.example: Define: Autoclave A device using pressurized steam for a validated sterilization cycle.

cards.back: Controlled heating that reduces pathogens and spoilage organisms without necessarily sterilizing a product.
cards.example: Does pasteurized mean sterile? No. Some viable organisms or spores may remain.

cards.back: No. Some viable organisms or spores may remain.
cards.example: Define: Pasteurization Controlled heating that reduces pathogens and spoilage organisms without necessarily sterilizing a product.

cards.back: A heritable ability of a bacterium to withstand an antimicrobial exposure that would inhibit susceptible bacteria.
cards.example: How can antibiotic use select resistance? Susceptible cells are suppressed while resistant variants survive and reproduce.

cards.front: How can antibiotic use select resistance?
cards.back: Susceptible cells are suppressed while resistant variants survive and reproduce.
cards.example: Define: Antibiotic resistance A heritable ability of a bacterium to withstand an antimicrobial exposure that would inhibit susceptible bacteria.

cards.back: Antimicrobial action that kills susceptible bacteria under specified conditions.
cards.example: How does bacteriostatic activity differ from bactericidal activity? Bacteriostatic activity inhibits growth; bactericidal activity kills, with effects dependent on organism and conditions.

cards.front: How does bacteriostatic activity differ from bactericidal activity?
cards.back: Bacteriostatic activity inhibits growth; bactericidal activity kills, with effects dependent on organism and conditions.
cards.example: Define: Bactericidal activity Antimicrobial action that kills susceptible bacteria under specified conditions.

cards.back: The lowest tested antimicrobial concentration preventing visible growth under standardized conditions.
cards.example: Is the MIC automatically the correct drug dose for a patient? No. Dosing also depends on pharmacology, infection site, patient factors, and validated interpretive criteria.

cards.front: Is the MIC automatically the correct drug dose for a patient?
cards.back: No. Dosing also depends on pharmacology, infection site, patient factors, and validated interpretive criteria.
cards.example: Define: Minimum inhibitory concentration The lowest tested antimicrobial concentration preventing visible growth under standardized conditions.

cards.back: A microbial protein toxin, often released by bacteria, that alters host cell functions.
cards.example: Can both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria produce exotoxins? Yes. Exotoxin production is not limited to one Gram-stain group.

cards.front: Can both Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria produce exotoxins?
cards.back: Yes. Exotoxin production is not limited to one Gram-stain group.
cards.example: Define: Exotoxin A microbial protein toxin, often released by bacteria, that alters host cell functions.

cards.back: Microorganisms usually associated with a particular body site.
cards.example: How can normal microbiota help resist pathogens? They can compete for nutrients and attachment sites and influence host defenses.

cards.front: How can normal microbiota help resist pathogens?
cards.back: They can compete for nutrients and attachment sites and influence host defenses.
cards.example: Define: Normal microbiota Microorganisms usually associated with a particular body site.

cards.back: An organism that causes disease especially when host defenses or normal barriers are impaired.
cards.example: Can a normal resident microbe become an opportunistic pathogen? Yes, for example after entering a normally sterile site or when immunity is impaired.

cards.front: Can a normal resident microbe become an opportunistic pathogen?
cards.back: Yes, for example after entering a normally sterile site or when immunity is impaired.
cards.example: Define: Opportunistic pathogen An organism that causes disease especially when host defenses or normal barriers are impaired.

cards.back: A eukaryotic organism that absorbs nutrients and usually has a chitin-containing cell wall.
cards.example: Which membrane sterol is characteristic of many fungi? Ergosterol, rather than the cholesterol typical of animal cell membranes.

cards.front: Which membrane sterol is characteristic of many fungi?
cards.back: Ergosterol, rather than the cholesterol typical of animal cell membranes.
cards.example: Define: Fungus A eukaryotic organism that absorbs nutrients and usually has a chitin-containing cell wall.

cards.back: A predominantly unicellular fungal growth form.
cards.example: How do many yeasts reproduce asexually? By budding, although some divide by fission.

cards.front: How do many yeasts reproduce asexually?
cards.back: By budding, although some divide by fission.
cards.example: Define: Yeast A predominantly unicellular fungal growth form.

cards.back: A filamentous fungal growth form made of hyphae.
cards.example: What is a mycelium? An interconnected mass of fungal hyphae.

cards.back: An interconnected mass of fungal hyphae.
cards.example: Define: Mold A filamentous fungal growth form made of hyphae.

cards.back: A tubular fungal filament that grows and absorbs nutrients.
cards.example: What is a septum in a fungal hypha? A cross-wall dividing the filament into compartments, often with pores.

cards.front: What is a septum in a fungal hypha?
cards.back: A cross-wall dividing the filament into compartments, often with pores.
cards.example: Define: Hypha A tubular fungal filament that grows and absorbs nutrients.

cards.back: A fungus capable of switching between distinct growth forms under different conditions.
cards.example: Is every dimorphic pathogenic fungus a yeast in tissue? No. For example, Coccidioides forms spherules in tissue rather than typical budding yeast.

cards.front: Is every dimorphic pathogenic fungus a yeast in tissue?
cards.back: No. For example, Coccidioides forms spherules in tissue rather than typical budding yeast.
cards.example: Define: Dimorphic fungus A fungus capable of switching between distinct growth forms under different conditions.

cards.back: A reproductive or dispersal structure produced sexually or asexually by fungi.
cards.example: How do fungal spores differ from bacterial endospores in general function? Fungal spores commonly serve reproduction and dispersal; bacterial endospores chiefly serve survival.

cards.front: How do fungal spores differ from bacterial endospores in general function?
cards.back: Fungal spores commonly serve reproduction and dispersal; bacterial endospores chiefly serve survival.
cards.example: Define: Fungal spore A reproductive or dispersal structure produced sexually or asexually by fungi.

cards.back: A fungus adapted to colonize keratinized tissues such as skin, hair, and nails.
cards.example: Which structural protein is the main nutrient target of dermatophytes? Keratin.

cards.front: Which structural protein is the main nutrient target of dermatophytes?
cards.back: Keratin.
cards.example: Define: Dermatophyte A fungus adapted to colonize keratinized tissues such as skin, hair, and nails.
